title: Logit-Attention Divergence: Mitigating Position Bias in Multi-Image Retrieval via Attention-Guided Calibration
claim: The baseline's predictions collapse onto a few favored positions regardless of ground truth; our correction restores a clean diagonal.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmaps, left-to-right, shared axes, Vanilla vs Ours
description: Two 8x8 confusion-matrix heatmaps sit side by side. Rows are ground-truth position and columns are predicted position. Cell values are selection rates in percent, and darker blue means a higher rate. The left panel, titled Vanilla, is smeared and off-diagonal. Most mass falls in columns 5–7, and column 7 is darkest, with 91–99% for rows 6–8. Columns 4 and 8 are almost empty, which shows as vertical stripes. The right panel, titled Ours, has a sharp dark-blue diagonal with values from 90.7 to 99.8 and near-zero off-diagonal cells. A shared 'Predicted Position' label is centered below both panels, and a 'Ground Truth Position' label runs along the left edge. The eye goes first to the dark column on the left and then to the diagonal on the right.
caption: Confusion matrices for LLaVA-OneVision on the multiimage retrieval task (N = 8, Random setting). Cell values represent the selection rate (%), where darker blue indicates a higher selection rate. The Vanilla baseline (Left) shows vertical stripes due to severe position bias, while our method (Right) restores the diagonal pattern, demonstrating that predictions correctly align with the ground truth.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance in multi-image cross-modal retrieval, yet suffer from severe position bias, where predictions are dominated by input order rather than semantic relevance. Through empirical analysis, we identify a phenomenon termed Logit-Attention Divergence, in which output logits are heavily biased while internal attention maps remain well-aligned with relevant visual evidence. This observation reveals a fundamental limitation of existing logit-level calibration methods such as PriDe. Based on this insight, we propose a training-free, attention-guided debiasing framework that leverages intrinsic attention signals for instance-level correction at inference time, requiring only a minimal calibration set with negligible computational overhead. Experiments on MS-COCO-based benchmarks show that our method substantially improves permutation invariance and achieves state-of-the-art performance, enhancing accuracy by over 40\% compared to baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/brightXian/LAD.
